Use this sheet with [the exercise](exercise-student.html). Predict before reading the results, then explain in words. These figures use direct grid calculations of the posterior; no model fitting is needed.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(posterior)
library(here)
source(here("R/functions.R"))
source(here("R/course_data.R"))
source(here("R/course_utils.R"))
source(here("R/course_visuals.R"))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 4.5
)
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 14))
```

## More seedlings, same observed proportion

Survey A has 2 survivors out of 5 seedlings; Survey B has 20 out of 50. Both plots use the same prior, grid and
horizontal axis. Predict the difference before viewing the second figure.

```{r comparisons, fig.height=3.4}
p <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 101)
for (N in c(5, 50)) {
  y <- 0.4 * N
  prior <- dbeta(p, shape1 = 1, shape2 = 1)
  likelihood <- dbinom(x = y, size = N, prob = p)
  posterior <- prior * likelihood
  posterior <- posterior / sum(posterior)
  figure <- tibble(p = p, posterior = posterior) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = p, y = posterior)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, colour = "#d95f02") +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1)) +
    labs(
      x = "Survival probability p",
      y = "Posterior probability per grid point",
      title = paste(y, "survivors out of", N, "seedlings")
    )
  print(figure)
}
```

Both observed proportions are 0.4. Under this model and prior, the larger survey
gives a narrower posterior: less uncertainty about the survival probability.
The continuous posteriors approximated here are Beta(3,4) and Beta(21,31).
Their means are close, but not identical.

The larger survey provides more information about $p$, so its likelihood is more
concentrated. With the same flat prior, its posterior is also narrower.
Both figures show probability per grid point; compare horizontal widths.
